title: Brooklyn Rules
full_review:
"Brooklyn Rules" (City Lights) is a coming-of-age comedy-drama about three Catholic schoolboys facing young adulthood in the 1980s. The surface details of their ingrained piousness feels just right, down to the most devout of the trio habitually kissing his crucifix when passing a statue of Mary.

This keen eye and the young men's respect for the church doesn't necessarily make for a spiritual experience, however. Set against a backdrop of the 1980s mob wars, in which Mafia members John Gotti and Paul Castellano violently vied for control, "Brooklyn Rules" is awash in graphic beatings, gunplay and an unpunished revenge killing by one of the three lead characters.

Childhood friends Carmine Mancuso, Bobby Canzoneri and the half-Italian Michael Turner (played as adults by Scott Caan, Jerry Ferrara and Freddie Prinze Jr.) are more repulsed than fascinated by the "wise guys" who control the commercial garbage business and skim from bingo night. Michael, who's enrolled at Columbia University, works nights in a butcher shop and dates nice WASP Ellen (Mena Suvari), is going to escape the neighborhood.

Bobby is an amiable slacker who lives at home. Carmine, however, is headed for trouble in the form of mob lieutenant Caesar Manganaro (Alec Baldwin, equal parts scary and charming).

Caesar is a well-tailored charmer who breaks legs without breaking a sweat, as a horrified Michael discovers one night when Caesar and Carmine drag in a rival to the mob's garbage cartel and -- thankfully, off-screen -- torture him. Caesar fortunately views Michael as a nice boy from the neighborhood who won't cause trouble.

And, in fact, Michael doesn't. He knows that in his neighborhood you keep your mouth shut or die, and so turns a blind eye to the immorality around him. While that troubled conscience elevates "Brooklyn Rules" above pulp melodrama, and the movie emphasizes how friendships can transcend time and circumstances, director Michael Corrente's film lacks the depth of "The Sopranos." (Screenwriter Terence Winter is, in fact, an executive producer of that series.)

The film contains pervasive rough and crude language; mild sexual innuendo and one nongraphic sex scene; much violence, including gunfire and beatings, with bloodshed; and a revenge killing without consequences. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
